paras: The killing of Ed McElroy took place at Frankfort, Kentucky, on the afternoon of August 7, 1882, a local election day, when a crowd at the polls shot dead McElroy, a Black man, after he fired a gun while officers tried to arrest him. The shot from McElroy's gun seriously wounded a man named Bud, or Sanford, Egbert. Telegraph dispatches carried the story across the country within days, most under headlines that cast McElroy as a "desperado" or "murderer."

Frankfort held its local elections that Monday, and the same dispatch that reported the shooting listed the new sheriff, city judge and city marshal. According to the Frankfort dispatch, McElroy quarreled with another Black man after the polls closed and went home for a shotgun "to renew the attack." A Louisville dispatch instead said he was "under the influence of election whisky" and became involved in a difficulty when Officer Hyde tried to arrest him.

In the Louisville version, McElroy ran to his house nearby, came out with an old musket, and pointed it toward the crowd at the polls from the mouth of an alley. When Officers Hyde and Darnell started toward him, he ran back into the alley, and the load of shot struck Sanford Egbert, who was passing. The Frankfort dispatch said simply that McElroy fired when an officer tried to arrest him, wounding Egbert, who was with the officer.

The crowd then opened fire on McElroy, and he fell dead at the scene. The Louisville wire put the officers among the shooters, saying "the officers and many others" fired and "completely riddled him." A later news-in-brief version said about twenty persons drew pistols after McElroy fired into the crowd.

The Frankfort Yeoman later reported that a large bullet had pierced a memorandum book in Egbert's left breast pocket, which it said saved his life. No report of an inquest, arrest or legal inquiry into McElroy's death appears in the coverage.

Only the white press covered the killing, and nearly all of it came from two short telegraph dispatches, one dated Frankfort and one Louisville, printed on August 8. Headline writers presented McElroy as the aggressor: the Savannah Morning News ran "A Negro Desperado Shot," the New-York Tribune "A Kentucky Murderer Killed," and the San Antonio Evening Light "Desperate Darkey." The two Wheeling papers blamed drink, under the heads "What Election Whisky Did" and "Running a Muck," while the St. Paul Globe headed its item "In True Kentucky Style."

A condensed news-in-brief version followed in weeklies such as the Kenosha Telegraph on August 11 and the Batesville Guard in Arkansas on August 16. In Kentucky, the Maysville Evening Bulletin gave the story one sentence, and the Hartford Herald reprinted the Yeoman's item about Egbert with the quip "Wonder the memorandum book hadn't been a bible." None of the reports questioned the killing or named anyone who fired.

Accounts differ on Egbert's role: the Frankfort dispatch placed him with the officers, the Louisville dispatch called him a passer-by, and two briefs called him an officer. The Wood River Times reversed the sequence, reporting that McElroy was wounded by "an officer named Bud Egbert" before a posse killed him, a version no other report supports. The Louisville wire said Egbert was shot in the head with shot, while the Frankfort Yeoman described a large bullet stopped at his breast pocket.

reader.title: Killing of Ed McElroy
bases: An election-day crowd at Frankfort, said in one version to include the officers, shot dead a Black man who had fired a gun while officers tried to arrest him (A1, A3, A13).

A Frankfort wire (A1, A4), a separate Louisville wire (A3, A7), a Maysville local item (A8) and the Frankfort Yeoman quoted in A14 agree that McElroy shot Egbert and was killed by gunfire from the crowd, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Frankfort wire
accounts.gist: After a quarrel with another Black man once the polls closed, McElroy went home for a shotgun to renew the attack; when an officer tried to arrest him he fired, wounding Bud Egbert, who was with the officer, and the crowd then fired and killed him.

accounts.label: Louisville wire
accounts.gist: McElroy, drunk on 'election whisky', ran from Officer Hyde to his house, came out with an old musket and pointed it at the crowd at the polls; as Hyde and Darnell approached he ran back into the alley, the shot struck Sanford Egbert as he passed, and the officers and many others riddled McElroy.

accounts.label: Weekly news-in-brief
accounts.gist: McElroy fired a double-barreled shotgun into the crowd at the polls and then at Sanford Egbert, after which about twenty persons drew pistols and killed him.

accounts.label: Inverted brief
accounts.gist: McElroy was seriously wounded by an officer named Bud Egbert, and a posse then fired on him and killed him.

accounts.label: Frankfort Yeoman
accounts.gist: A large bullet pierced a memorandum book in Egbert's left breast pocket, which saved his life.

framing.detail: Headlines cast McElroy as the aggressor: 'A Negro Desperado Shot' (Savannah), 'A Kentucky Murderer Killed' (New-York Tribune), 'Desperate Darkey' (San Antonio).
Most papers ran one of two short wires or a weekly brief without comment; the Wheeling papers blamed 'election whisky'.
The St. Paul Globe headed the item 'In True Kentucky Style', and the Hartford Herald joked about Egbert's memorandum book.
